findings.symptom: The screenshot title renders “tau” and “log n” as plain words, although they are mathematical notation.
findings.suggested_repair: Mark the symbols explicitly, for example “The average order of $\tau$ is $\log n$”.

findings.symptom: The title shows literal ASCII “Z_p” rather than a typeset p-adic ring symbol.
The title shows “Q(i)” as plain ASCII instead of the number-field notation used in the body.
The title renders “[1; overline 2]” and “sqrt(2)” as literal ASCII formula text.
The title renders “Z[sqrt 5]” literally; the radical and number ring are not typeset.
The title renders “Z[sqrt 5]” and “O_Q(sqrt 5)” as literal ASCII formula text.
The title renders “Q_p” literally with an underscore rather than typeset p-adic field notation.
The technique banner prints raw inline TeX delimiters and commands, including “$r_1+r_2-1$” and “$\mathcal O_K^\times\cong...$”, instead of rendering them.
findings.suggested_repair: Remove TeX markup from the non-math technique field or rewrite the banner in plain words (for example, “read the unit rank from Dirichlet’s unit theorem”).

findings.symptom: The verification technique banner prints the polynomial with literal dollar delimiters and TeX syntax (“$X^3-3X+1$”).
findings.suggested_repair: Rewrite the non-math technique field in plain text, for example “the cubic polynomial X^3 - 3X + 1,” or move formula notation into a rendered prose field.

findings.symptom: The verification technique banner prints raw inline TeX for “$N(u)=\pm1$” rather than typesetting the norm equation.
findings.suggested_repair: Rewrite this non-math technique field in plain text (“the norm equation N(u) = plus or minus 1”) or put the formula in a rendered prose field.

diagram_candidates.construction: Plot the finite integer points with 1 <= x <= (p-1)/2 and 0 < p y < q x; show the sloping boundary py=qx and distinguish counted points. Check that open/closed boundary treatment and the strict inequality match the source set exactly.
diagram_candidates.why_source_supports_it: The statement explicitly defines Gauss’s sign as the parity of a finite two-dimensional lattice-point set.

diagram_candidates.construction: Draw the open integer rectangle 1 <= x <= (p-1)/2, 1 <= y <= (q-1)/2, the diagonal py=qx, and the two disjoint point sets py<qx and qx<py with labels S_{p,q}, S_{q,p}. Check there are no diagonal lattice points because p and q are distinct primes, and that exchanging coordinates/primes swaps the regions.
diagram_candidates.why_source_supports_it: The proof partitions the rectangle into exactly the two lower-half lattice counts; the relation is geometric and a diagram could clarify the partition.
